capstone: Build a complete 'MiniMart' order-processing database on SQL Server 2022 Developer edition (free download) or the Azure SQL free tier — no paid licenses required. Deliver: (1) schema with constraints; (2) a stored procedure that places an order (input params, OUTPUT order id, TRY/CATCH transaction, THROW on stock shortage); (3) an inline TVF for customer order history consumed via CROSS APPLY; (4) an AFTER trigger auditing price changes; (5) a dynamic-search procedure using sp_executesql with injection tests documented; (6) Query Store enabled with a baseline captured and one deliberate regression identified and fixed via plan forcing. Ship a README with setup steps, the attack/defense transcript from module 7, and your 5-step slow-database runbook from module 8.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Without looking: rewrite `SELECT * FROM Orders ORDER BY Id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` in two T-SQL ways, and state which is guaranteed deterministic.
Explain to an imaginary Postgres peer why `WHERE Name = 'enmanuel'` and `WHERE Name = N'enmanuel'` can behave differently on a varchar column with a non-default collation.
List three T-SQL-isms that would silently change meaning (not just error) if pasted into a standard-SQL engine.
keyConcepts: TOP (n) vs LIMIT; OFFSET/FETCH as the ANSI paging path
Bracketed [identifiers] vs double-quoted identifiers vs QUOTED_IDENTIFIER
NULL handling quirks and collation-dependent string comparison
SET options (ANSI_NULLS, ANSI_PADDING) and why legacy databases break without them
N-prefix for Unicode literals (N'text') and the nvarchar default habit
@@ variables, system functions, and catalog views as dialect surface area
labs: Run the same paging query three ways — TOP, OFFSET/FETCH, and a ROW_NUMBER() window — and compare plans and logical reads; record which one you would use for a web grid.
Create two tables with different collations, run a JOIN and an equality filter, and document where the comparison fails or silently succeeds.
Write a porting exercise: take a 20-line MySQL/Postgres-flavored script (LIMIT, backticks, AUTO_INCREMENT, double-quoted aliases) and rewrite it in T-SQL, annotating each changed line with why.
Probe SET options: toggle ANSI_NULLS ON/OFF in a session and run NULL comparisons, then write a one-paragraph rule for how you will set session options in every new script.
objectives: Name the major T-SQL deviations from ANSI SQL syntax and semantics.
Predict how TOP, OFFSET/FETCH, and bracketed identifiers behave differently from other dialects.
Convert a LIMIT/OFFSET query and an ANSI quoting example into idiomatic T-SQL.
Explain when a 'portable' query is and isn't worth the effort.
modules.title: Module 1 — T-SQL vs Standard SQL: What's Actually Different

checkpoints: What does `SELECT @x = col FROM t` assign when `t` has 5 rows? Why is this a bug factory?
A variable works on line 10 but errors 'must declare' on line 12 — name the most likely cause in one sentence.
Table variable vs #temp table: state one scenario where each is the better choice, with the reason.
keyConcepts: DECLARE/SET/SELECT assignment and the multi-row SELECT-assignment trap
Batches, GO, and why a variable dies at the batch boundary
IF/ELSE, WHILE loops, CASE expressions vs CASE statements
Table variables vs #temp tables: scope, statistics, and recompilation trade-offs
PRINT vs SELECT for debugging; RAISERROR (low severity) for progress messages
labs: Build a scratch-lab script that declares variables, assigns them via both SET and SELECT, then deliberately crosses a GO boundary — capture the exact error and write the fix in a comment.

Write a WHILE loop that processes a 1,000-row staging table in 100-row batches using a table variable as the work queue; add BREAK on an error flag and verify no infinite loop when the table is empty.

Performance comparison lab: load 50k rows into a table variable and into a #temp table, join each against a real table, and compare estimated vs actual row counts in the plans; write the rule of thumb you would teach.
Refactor a 40-line batch that repeats the same subquery three times into one that computes it once into a variable; measure logical reads before and after.
objectives: Declare, assign, and scope variables correctly across batches and GO boundaries.
Use IF/ELSE, WHILE, CASE, and the BREAK/CONTINUE pattern without infinite loops.
Choose between scalar variables, table variables, and temp tables for scratch data.
Debug a batch by reading messages, PRINT output, and the actual execution plan.
modules.title: Module 2 — Variables, Batches, and Control of Flow

checkpoints: OUTPUT parameter vs RETURN code vs result set: give one correct use for each.
Your procedure is fast for customer A and 50x slower for customer B on the same code path — what is the prime suspect and what is the cheapest experiment to confirm it?
Why does calling with named parameters (`@CustomerId = 42`) make future refactoring safer than positional calls?
keyConcepts: Input vs OUTPUT parameters; RETURN codes are for status, not data
Default values, named vs positional invocation
Parameter sniffing: what it is, when it helps, when it wrecks a plan
Local-variable copy, OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN — trade-offs
Ownership chaining and the EXECUTE AS options at a high level
labs: Write usp_GetOrdersByCustomer with @CustomerId INT and @OrderCount INT OUTPUT; call it three ways (positional, named, with OUTPUT variable) and confirm the output value.

Parameter-sniffing lab: build a skewed table (one customer with 100k orders, many with 5), write a procedure filtering by @CustomerId, and observe the bad-plan flip by calling with different first parameters; fix it with a local-variable copy and re-measure.
Refactor a procedure that returns data via RETURN code into one using an OUTPUT parameter plus a status code; write a one-line comment at each call site explaining the convention.
Security lab: create a low-privilege login/user, grant only EXECUTE on your procedure, and verify the caller can get results without SELECT rights on the base table.
objectives: Write CREATE PROCEDURE with input parameters, OUTPUT parameters, and return codes used correctly.
Apply parameter defaults, named invocation, and the OUTPUT keyword at the call site.
Avoid the parameter-sniffing trap with local variables, OPTIMIZE FOR, or RECOMPILE — and know the cost of each.
Grant EXECUTE without granting direct table access (ownership chaining basics).
modules.title: Module 3 — Stored Procedures: Input, Output, and Return

checkpoints: Why can the same logic run 100x faster as an inline TVF than as a scalar UDF in a SELECT list?
When would you deliberately choose a multi-statement TVF despite its optimizer cost?
Rewrite a correlated scalar subquery in the SELECT clause as a CROSS APPLY against an inline TVF — do it from memory.
keyConcepts: Scalar UDFs: row-by-row execution and why they poison query plans (pre-2019) and scalar UDF inlining (2019+)
Inline TVFs: parameterizable views the optimizer can fold in
Multi-statement TVFs: flexible but opaque to the optimizer (fixed cardinality guesses)
CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY as the TVF join pattern
Determinism and schemabinding where it matters
labs: Write a scalar UDF that formats an order total, use it in a SELECT over 100k rows, and time it; then rewrite as an inline TVF with CROSS APPLY and compare elapsed time and plans.
Build an inline TVF TopOrders(@CustomerId, @N) returning the N most recent orders; consume it with CROSS APPLY over a customer list and verify the plan stays a single efficient shape.

Multi-statement TVF lab: write one that builds a result via a table variable and control flow, use it in a join, and observe the plan's row estimate vs actual; write the sentence you would put in a code review.

Decision lab: for five small requirements (lookup formatting, parameterized report slice, audit stamp, running total, permission-filtered rowset) pick function/procedure/view and defend each choice in one line.
objectives: Write scalar, inline table-valued, and multi-statement table-valued functions, and state the performance profile of each.
Predict where a scalar UDF in a WHERE/SELECT will kill performance and rewrite it.
Use CROSS APPLY with an inline TVF to replace a correlated subquery.
Decide function vs procedure vs view for a given requirement.
modules.title: Module 4 — User-Defined Functions: Scalar and Table-Valued

checkpoints: Your trigger works in testing but misses rows in production — what is the single most likely cause?
INSTEAD OF trigger on a view: who performs the actual base-table writes, and what happens to the original INSERT?
Name one rule that belongs in a CHECK constraint, one that belongs in a trigger, and one that belongs in the application — with the reason for each.
keyConcepts: inserted and deleted: set-based, possibly multi-row — never assume one row
AFTER (FOR) vs INSTEAD OF: timing, what each can and cannot do
UPDATE() and COLUMNS_UPDATED() for column-level logic
Nested triggers, recursive triggers, and sp_configure 'nested triggers'
Why triggers hide logic: debugging, performance, and the case for constraints first
labs: Write an AFTER UPDATE trigger that logs every price change to an audit table with old/new values, user, and timestamp; test with a single-row and a 500-row UPDATE and verify both log correctly.
INSTEAD OF lab: create a view joining two tables, make it updatable with an INSTEAD OF INSERT trigger that splits the row correctly; then attempt a bad insert and confirm your validation fires.
Multi-row trap lab: write a trigger that naively assumes one row in inserted (scalar variable assignment), fire it with a 3-row insert, and document exactly what breaks; then fix it set-based.

Recursion lab: on a scratch database, create two tables with triggers that update each other, enable recursive triggers, run one update, and observe; then write the guard (trigger_nestlevel or a flag table) you would ship.
objectives: Write AFTER triggers using the inserted/deleted pseudo-tables for multi-row operations.
Use INSTEAD OF triggers to make non-updatable views updatable and to enforce complex rules.
Explain trigger firing order, nesting, and recursion settings and their dangers.
Argue for and against triggers vs constraints vs application logic for a given rule.
modules.title: Module 5 — Triggers: DML and INSTEAD OF

checkpoints: After a CATCH block runs ROLLBACK, what is @@TRANCOUNT and why does that matter to the caller?
THROW; with no arguments inside a CATCH block does what — and why is that better than RAISERROR with a copied message?
A procedure opens a transaction, calls another procedure that also has BEGIN/COMMIT TRAN — how many real transactions are there, and what does the inner COMMIT actually do?
keyConcepts: TRY/CATCH scope: what is catchable, batch-aborting vs statement-aborting errors
ERROR_NUMBER/MESSAGE/SEVERITY/STATE/LINE/PROCEDURE in the CATCH block
THROW (no args) re-throw vs RAISERROR; custom error numbers >= 50000
BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK TRAN, @@TRANCOUNT, and the nested-transaction myth
SET XACT_ABORT ON and why most production procedures want it
labs: Write a money-transfer-style procedure (debit A, credit B) with TRY/CATCH; inject a failure between the two statements and prove with @@TRANCOUNT and a balance query that no partial commit survives.
XACT_ABORT lab: run the same failing batch with XACT_ABORT OFF and ON, and document the difference in what rolls back; write the one-paragraph rule for your team's template.

Error-context lab: catch a divide-by-zero and a foreign-key violation, and build a logging procedure that records ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_LINE(), and ERROR_PROCEDURE(); verify the log row for both.
Idempotency lab: write a staging-to-fact loader that can be re-run safely after a mid-load failure (checkpoints table or MERGE semantics), and test by killing it halfway twice.
objectives: Structure TRY/CATCH blocks so no error path leaves a transaction open.
Use THROW vs RAISERROR correctly and re-throw with original context preserved.
Pair XACT_ABORT with explicit transactions and know what each setting changes.
Write an idempotent, retry-safe data-load procedure with proper rollback semantics.
modules.title: Module 6 — Error Handling: TRY/CATCH, THROW, and Transactions

checkpoints: Why does sp_executesql with parameters defeat `' OR 1=1 --` while string concatenation does not? Answer at the level of how the engine treats the input.
You must accept a table name from the user. List the two safe approaches in order of preference.
A dynamic pivot query is slow on every run — what plan-cache behavior explains it, and what is the standard mitigation?
keyConcepts: sp_executesql with @params: plan reuse and type safety
EXEC('...') string concatenation: the injection surface
QUOTENAME() for identifiers; parameterize values, quote names, never mix
Classic payloads: `' OR 1=1 --`, stacked queries, and why parameterization kills them
Dynamic SQL scope: temp tables and variables don't cross the EXEC boundary
labs: Vulnerable-then-fixed lab: write a search procedure that concatenates @SearchTerm into the SQL string; attack it with `' OR '1'='1` and a stacked `DROP TABLE` on a scratch table; then rewrite with sp_executesql parameters and re-run both attacks to prove they fail.

QUOTENAME lab: write a procedure that takes a @TableName and returns row counts; first version concatenates raw (demonstrate injection via a crafted name), fixed version uses QUOTENAME; also show the allow-list alternative.

Optional-filter lab: build a report procedure with 5 optional filters three ways — dynamic SQL with sp_executesql, static SQL with `(@p IS NULL OR col = @p)`, and OPTION (RECOMPILE); compare plans and reads on skewed data and write the guidance.
Scope lab: create a #temp table in the outer batch, try to read it inside sp_executesql (works — same session), then try to reference an outer variable (fails); document the rule.
objectives: Build dynamic SQL with sp_executesql and strongly-typed parameters instead of EXEC().
Sanitize object names with QUOTENAME and never concatenate user input into identifiers raw.
Demonstrate a working injection attack on a lab database, then close it.
Decide when dynamic SQL is justified (optional filters, dynamic pivots, DDL automation) vs when static SQL wins.
modules.title: Module 7 — Dynamic SQL and Injection Defense

checkpoints: Query Store shows two plan_ids for one query_id with very different avg durations — what happened, and what are your two remediation options?
Why is forcing a plan a treatment rather than a cure? State what you must still investigate.
Name the three SET/SHOW outputs you capture before asking anyone for help with a slow query.
keyConcepts: SSMS vs Azure Data Studio: when each shines; both are free
Actual execution plans, live query stats, SET STATISTICS IO/TIME
Query Store: query_id/plan_id model, runtime stats, wait categories
Regressed queries report and plan forcing (and when to un-force)
Baselines: capturing 'normal' before you need it
labs: Tooling setup lab: install SSMS (or Azure Data Studio), configure 'Include Actual Execution Plan' shortcut, save two code snippets (TRY/CATCH transaction template, sp_executesql template), and connect to your lab instance.

Query Store lab: on a scratch database enable Query Store, run a workload 20 times to build history, then force a bad plan (hint or stats change) and find the regression in the 'Regressed Queries' view; force the good plan and verify recovery.

Slow-database drill: pick your slowest lab query from Module 4, capture its plan + STATISTICS IO/TIME output as a baseline file, then write the 5-step runbook you would follow if a teammate reported it slow tomorrow.
Cross-tool lab: do the same plan capture in both SSMS and Azure Data Studio and note one thing each tool does better for your workflow.
objectives: Set up a productive SSMS or Azure Data Studio workflow: templates, snippets, actual plans, and client statistics.
Enable and read Query Store: regressed queries, wait stats, and plan forcing.
Capture a baseline, introduce a regression on purpose, and identify it in Query Store.
Write a personal runbook: the 5 checks you run when 'the database is slow'.
modules.title: Module 8 — SSMS / Azure Data Studio Workflow and Query Store Basics

objectives: Write correct, readable T-SQL across batches, variables, control-of-flow, procedures, functions, and triggers without relying on vendor-specific habits from other databases.
Design stored procedures and user-defined functions with safe parameter handling, and defend against SQL injection in dynamic SQL.
Handle errors and transactions reliably with TRY/CATCH and THROW, and diagnose plan regressions with Query Store in SSMS or Azure Data Studio.
